notes.meaning: David escaped from Gath to the cave of Adullam, near his home territory in Judah. His brothers and the rest of his family heard about it and joined him there to escape Saul's anger. David was hiding in a rough cave, but he trusted God as his true shelter.

About four hundred men who were in trouble, deep in debt, or bitter in spirit gathered around David. Instead of leading an angry mob, David trained them into a disciplined and honest company. His care for these broken men pictures how Jesus warmly receives all who are weary and burdened.

David traveled to Moab to ask the king of Moab for shelter for his elderly parents. David's great-grandmother was Ruth the Moabitess, so his family had kinship ties with that country. He humbly left his parents in safety until he could learn what God would do for him.

David left his parents under the care of the king of Moab while he remained on the run. The elderly couple could not survive the hardships and dangers of wandering through wilderness hideouts. David's tender care reminds us to honor and protect our parents in difficult times.

The prophet Gad told David to leave his mountain fortress and return to the land of Judah. God guided David through the prophet, calling him to show trust in the Lord rather than hide away in a foreign land. David obeyed immediately and moved into the forest of Hereth.

Saul received word that David and his band of men had been spotted in Judah. The king held court under a tamarisk tree on a hill at Gibeah, holding his spear like a royal sceptre while his officers stood around him. He ruled from fear and suspicion, watching nervously for threats to his throne.

Saul spoke sharply to the royal officers who belonged to his own tribe of Benjamin. He asked whether David, a man from the tribe of Judah, could ever hand out fields, vineyards, and high military ranks to them as Saul had done. Saul tried to play on their tribal pride and greed to keep their loyalty.

Saul angrily accused his officers of plotting against him and hiding Jonathan's close bond with David. In his paranoid jealousy, Saul imagined that his own son had urged David to lie in wait to kill him. Saul felt sorry for himself and blamed innocent people for a conspiracy that did not exist.

Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen, spoke up to win favor and promotion from the king. He reported that he had seen David visit the high priest Ahimelech at the sanctuary in Nob. Doeg harbored malice toward David and jumped at the chance to accuse him before Saul.

Doeg told Saul that Ahimelech had asked God for guidance for David, given him provisions, and handed him Goliath's sword. While these actions really happened, Doeg twisted them into an act of treason. He left out the fact that David had tricked the priest by claiming to be on the king's secret business.

Saul sent messengers to summon Ahimelech and the entire priestly family living at Nob. All the priests came promptly to the king because their consciences were completely clear of wrongdoing. Without knowing it, Saul's wicked summons was moving forward God's ancient judgment against the family of Eli.

Saul addressed the high priest with contempt, calling him only the son of Ahitub rather than using his name or holy title. Ahimelech answered with humble respect, saying, 'Here I am, my lord.' The priest stood ready to hear the charges because he knew he had acted in good faith.

Saul charged Ahimelech with high treason for helping David with bread, a weapon, and prayer. He claimed that the high priest was helping David ambush and overthrow him. Saul's blind rage caused him to see ordinary hospitality as a deadly plot against the crown.

Ahimelech defended David with quiet dignity, asking who in the whole kingdom was as faithful as David. He reminded Saul that David was the king's son-in-law, the head of his bodyguard, and highly honored in the palace. Ahimelech explained that he had helped David simply out of loyalty to Saul's household.

Ahimelech explained that seeking God's guidance for David was nothing new, as he had often done so during David's royal missions. He asked the king not to accuse him or his family of rebellion, because he knew nothing at all about any quarrel. Ahimelech spoke the honest truth, having acted in complete innocence.

Saul brushed aside the priest's defense and sentenced Ahimelech and his whole family to die. This hasty ruling was an act of terrible tyranny against innocent servants of God. Even though Saul acted out of sinful fury, God permitted it to fulfill his word against the house of Eli.

Saul commanded his royal runners to kill the priests of the Lord, claiming they had sided with a fugitive. However, the king's guards refused to raise their hands against God's consecrated priests. They rightly recognized that obeying God came before obeying an evil command from an earthly king.

Saul ordered Doeg to carry out the executions, and Doeg struck down the priests on the spot. He murdered eighty-five men wearing the linen ephod, the sacred white garment worn by priests during holy service. Being an Edomite who did not fear the Lord, Doeg felt no horror at killing God's ministers.

Doeg then attacked the priestly city of Nob, slaughtering men, women, children, infants, and farm animals with the sword. Saul had earlier refused to destroy the wicked Amalekites when God commanded it, but now he showed no mercy to the innocent families of God's priests. His cruel revenge wiped out an entire town over a groundless suspicion.

Abiathar, one of Ahimelech's sons, escaped the slaughter and fled to David's camp. He brought along the high priest's sacred vestment, which was used to ask God for direction. God preserved Abiathar, fulfilling his promise that a small remnant of Eli's family would survive.

Abiathar reached David and told him that Saul had slaughtered the priests of the Lord. The terrible report showed how completely Saul was controlled by an evil and violent spirit. David was filled with grief to learn that the sanctuary town had been wiped out.

David told Abiathar that he had feared Doeg would betray him the moment he saw him at Nob. He openly confessed that his own deceit had brought about the deaths of the priests. David showed true integrity by taking full responsibility for the tragedy his lie had caused.

David urged Abiathar to stay with him and not be afraid, promising to guard his life. Since Saul was hunting both of them, David pledged that they would face the danger together and remain safe. In this way, God brought the future king and the future high priest together as companions in the wilderness.
